entries.ebe4f47eef93702d9721806d7bce08177d141a63: <div sID="gen13698" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Prov.12" sID="Prov.12"/> <div eID="gen13698" type="x-p"/>
entries.97175d1563f104e2d011bd0052b16371a243c60b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv27"/><title type="x-s3">Advantages of the Righteous.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv27"/> <div sID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof <hi type="italic">is</hi> brutish. <div eID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> We are here taught to try whether we have grace or no by enquiring how we stand affected to the means of grace. 1. Those that have grace and love it will delight in all the instructions that are given them by way of counsel; admonition, or reproof, by the word or providence of God; they will value a good education, and think it not a hardship, but a happiness, to be under a strict and prudent discipline. Those that love a faithful ministry, that value it, and sit under it with pleasure, make it to appear that they <hi type="italic">love knowledge.</hi> 2. Those show themselves not only void of grace, but void of common sense, that take it as an affront to be told of their faults, and an imposition upon their liberty to be put in mind of their duty: <hi type="italic">He that hates reproof is</hi> not only foolish, but <hi type="italic">brutish,</hi> like the horse and the mule that have no understanding, or the ox that kicks against the goad. Those that desire to live in loose families and societies, where they may be under no check, that stifle the convictions of their own consciences, and count those their enemies that tell them the truth, are the <hi type="italic">brutish</hi> here meant.
entries.90a338e179319151bfa56da691be202af401fdd6: <div eID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> A good <hi type="italic">man</hi> obtaineth favour of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but a man of wicked devices will he condemn. <div eID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13702" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We are really as we are with God. Those are happy, truly happy, for ever happy, that <hi type="italic">obtain favour of the Lord,</hi> though the world frown upon them, and they find little favour with men; for in God's favour is life, and that is the fountain of all good. On the other hand those are miserable whom <hi type="italic">he condemns,</hi> however men may applaud them, and cry them up; whom he condemns he condemns to the second death. 2. We are with God as we are with men, as we have our conversation in this world. Our Father judges of his children very much by their conduct one to another; and therefore <hi type="italic">a good man,</hi> that is merciful, and charitable, and does good, <hi type="italic">draws out favour from the Lord</hi> by his prayers; but a malicious man, that devises wickedness against his neighbours, <hi type="italic">he will condemn,</hi> as unworthy of a place in his kingdom.
entries.790eb73fc3818f84a1e957faac30e1bf12caebf1: <div eID="gen13702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved. <div eID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Though men may advance themselves by sinful arts, they cannot by such arts settle and secure themselves; though they may get large estates they cannot get such as will abide: <hi type="italic">A man shall not be established by wickedness;</hi> it may set him in high places, but they are slippery places, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.18">Ps. lxxiii. 18</reference>. That prosperity which is raised by sin is built on the sand, and so it will soon appear. 2. Though good men may have but little of the world, yet that little will last, and what is honestly got will wear well: <hi type="italic">The root of the righteous shall not be moved,</hi> though their branches may be shaken. Those that by faith are rooted in Christ are firmly fixed; in him their comfort and happiness are so rooted as never to be rooted up.
entries.29d8d51350ed957496628d35e47ed07a4d75a8fe: <div eID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> A virtuous woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed <hi type="italic">is</hi> as rottenness in his bones. <div eID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13706" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He that is blessed with a good wife is as happy as if he were upon the throne, for she is no less than <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> to him. <hi type="italic">A virtuous woman,</hi> that is pious and prudent, ingenious and industrious, that is active for the good of her family and looks well to the ways of her household, that makes conscience of her duty in every relation, a woman of spirit, that can bear crosses without disturbance, such a one owns her husband for her head, and therefore she <hi type="italic">is a crown</hi> to him, not only a credit and honour to him, as <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> is an ornament, but supports and keeps up his authority in his family, as <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> is an ensign of power. She is submissive and faithful to him and by her example teaches his children and servants to be so too. 2. He that is plagued with a bad wife is as miserable as if he were upon the dunghill; for she is no better than <hi type="italic">rottenness in his bones,</hi> an incurable disease, besides that <hi type="italic">she makes him ashamed.</hi> She that is silly and slothful, wasteful and wanton, passionate and ill-tongued, ruins both the credit and comfort of her husband. If he go abroad, his head is hung down, for his wife's faults turn to his reproach. If he retire into himself, his heart is sunk; he is continually uneasy; it is an affliction that preys much upon the spirits.
entries.4f25904b730d6c9908d4e2cde6834deab5b8b9f6: <div eID="gen13706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13707" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> The thoughts of the righteous <hi type="italic">are</hi> right: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the counsels of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> deceit. <div eID="gen13707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The word of God is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart, and judges them. We mistake if we imagine that thoughts are free. No, they are under the divine cognizance, and therefore under the divine command. 2. We ought to be observers of the thoughts and intents of our own hearts, and to judge of ourselves by them; for they are the first-born of the soul, that have most of its image undisguised. Right thoughts are a righteous man's best evidences, as nothing more certainly proves a man wicked than wicked contrivances and designs. A good man may have in his mind bad suggestions, but he does not indulge them and harbour them till they are ripened into bad projects and resolutions. 3. It is a man's honour to mean honestly, and to have his thoughts right, though a word or action may be misplaced, or mistimed, or at least misinterpreted. But it is a man's shame to lie always at catch, to act with deceit, with trick and design, not only with a long reach, but with an overreach.
entries.da986196fc73feeeadcd9757fd7cb3a065c47b6a: <div eID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> The words of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them. <div eID="gen13709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> In the foregoing verse the <hi type="italic">thoughts</hi> of the wicked and righteous were compared; here their <hi type="italic">words,</hi> and those are as the abundance of the heart is. 1. Wicked people speak mischief to their neighbours; and wicked indeed those are whose <hi type="italic">words</hi> are to <hi type="italic">lie in wait for blood;</hi> their tongues are swords to those that stand in their way, to good men whom they hate and persecute. See an instance, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20-Luke.20.21">Luke xx. 20, 21</reference>. 2. Good men speak help to their neighbours: The <hi type="italic">mouth of the upright</hi> is ready to be opened in the cause of those that are oppressed (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.8">ch. xxxi. 8</reference>), to plead for them, to witness for them, and so to <hi type="italic">deliver them,</hi> particularly those whom the wicked <hi type="italic">lie in wait</hi> for. A man may sometimes do a very good work with one good word.
entries.33d93bc0e6cdcdc43427c738e8861787fc779270: <div eID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The wicked are overthrown, and <hi type="italic">are</hi> not: but the house of the righteous shall stand. <div eID="gen13711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> We are here taught as before (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.3 Prov.10.25 Prov.10.30">v. 3 and ch. x. 25, 30</reference>), 1. That the <hi type="italic">triumphing of the wicked is short.</hi> They may be exalted for a while, but in a little time they are <hi type="italic">overthrown and are not;</hi> their trouble proves their overthrow, and those who made a great show disappear, and their place knows them no more. <hi type="italic">Turn the wicked, and they are not;</hi> they stand in such a slippery place that the least touch of trouble brings them down, like the apples of Sodom, which look fair, but touch them and they go to dust. 2. That the prosperity of the righteous has a good bottom and will endure. Death will remove them, but their <hi type="italic">house</hi> shall <hi type="italic">stand,</hi> their families shall be kept up, and the generation of the upright shall be blessed.
entries.78ee824e1194c89aed3ebed8bf6d9709666bce87: <div eID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised. <div eID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> We are here told whence to expect a good name. Reputation is what most have a high regard to and stand much upon. Now it is certain, 1. The best reputation is that which attends virtue and serious piety, and the prudent conduct of life: <hi type="italic">A man shall be commended</hi> by all that are wise and good, in conformity to the judgment of God himself, which we are sure is <hi type="italic">according to truth,</hi> not according to his riches or preferments, his craft and subtlety, but <hi type="italic">according to his wisdom,</hi> the honesty of his designs and the prudent choice of means to compass them. 2. The worst reproach is that which follows wickedness and an opposition to that which is good: <hi type="italic">He that is of a perverse heart,</hi> that turns aside to crooked ways, and goes on frowardly in them, <hi type="italic">shall be despised.</hi> Providence will bring him to poverty and contempt, and all that have a true sense of honour will despise him as unworthy to be dealt with and unfit to be trusted, as a blemish and scandal to mankind.
entries.3db2dd9af582d3b1ff65f16855667d31d3a82c66: <div eID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> despised, and hath a servant, <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread. <div eID="gen13715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is the folly of some that they covet to make a great figure abroad, take place, and take state, as persons of quality, and yet want necessaries at home, and, if their debts were paid, would not be worth a morsel of bread, nay, perhaps, pinch their bellies to put it on their backs, that they may appear very gay, because fine feathers make fine birds. 2. The condition and character of those is every way better who content themselves in a lower sphere, where they are despised for the plainness of their dress and the meanness of their post, that they may be able to afford themselves, not only necessaries, but conveniences, in their own houses, not only bread, but a servant to attend them and take some of their work off their hands. Those that contrive to live plentifully and comfortably at home are to be preferred before those that affect nothing so much as to appear splendid abroad, though they have not wherewithal to maintain their appearance, whose hearts are unhumbled when their condition is low.
entries.944a0235f5698f50a547b47a892279a35587d926: <div eID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> A righteous <hi type="italic">man</hi> regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> cruel. <div eID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13718" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. To how great a degree a good man will be merciful; he has not only a compassion for the human nature under its greatest abasements, but he regards even <hi type="italic">the life of his beast,</hi> not only because it is his servant, but because it is God's creature, and in conformity to Providence, which <hi type="italic">preserves man and beast.</hi> The beasts that are under our care must be provided for, must have convenient food and rest, must in no case be abused or tyrannised over. Balaam was checked for beating his ass. The law took care for oxen. Those therefore are unrighteous men that are not just to the brute-creatures; those that are furious and barbarous to them evidence, and confirm in themselves, a habit of barbarity, and help to make the creation groan, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 22</reference>. 2. To how great a degree a wicked man will be unmerciful; even his <hi type="italic">tender mercies</hi> are <hi type="italic">cruel;</hi> that natural compassion which is in him, as a man, is lost, and, by the power of corruption, is turned into hard-heartedness; even that which they will have to pass for compassion is really cruel, as Pilate's resolution concerning Christ the innocent, <hi type="italic">I will chastise him and let him go.</hi> Their pretended kindnesses are only a cover for purposed cruelties.
entries.0f92137aee9ef1f516ac5ba2940bcc15023aa108: <div eID="gen13718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13719" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain <hi type="italic">persons is</hi> void of understanding. <div eID="gen13719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13720" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is men's wisdom to mind their business and follow an honest calling, for that is the way, by the blessing of God, to get a livelihood: <hi type="italic">He that tills his land,</hi> of which he is either the owner or the occupant, that keeps to his word and is willing to take pains, if he do not raise an estate by it (what need is there of that?), yet he <hi type="italic">shall be satisfied with bread,</hi> shall have food convenient for himself and his family, enough to bear his charges comfortably through the world. Even the sentence of wrath has this mercy in it, Thou shalt <hi type="italic">eat bread,</hi> though it be <hi type="italic">in the sweat of thy face.</hi> Cain was denied this, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.12">Gen. iv. 12</reference>. Be busy, and that is the true way to be easy. Keep thy shop and thy shop will keep thee. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt eat the labour of thy hands.</hi> 2. It is men's folly to neglect their business. Those are <hi type="italic">void of understanding</hi> that do so, for then they fall in with idle companions and follow them in their evil courses, and so come to want bread, at least bread of their own, and make themselves burdensome to others, eating the bread out of other people's mouths.
entries.ec1d1f501457577728ffd619b561a06c6aabd561: <div eID="gen13720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13721" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The wicked desireth the net of evil <hi type="italic">men:</hi> but the root of the righteous yieldeth <hi type="italic">fruit.</hi> <div eID="gen13721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13722" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What is the care and aim of a wicked man; he would do mischief: He <hi type="italic">desires the net of evil men.</hi> "Oh that I were but as cunning as such a man, to make a hand of those I deal with, that I had but his art of over-reaching, that I could but take my revenge on one I have spite to as effectually as he can!" He desires the <hi type="italic">strong-hold, or fortress,</hi> of evil men (so some read it), to act securely in doing mischief, that it may not turn upon him. 2. What is the care and aim of a good man: His <hi type="italic">root yields fruit,</hi> and is his strength and stability, and that is it that he desires, to do good and to be fixed and confirmed in doing good. The wicked desires only a net wherewith to fish for himself; the righteous desires to yield fruit for the benefit of others and God's glory, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.6">Rom. xiv. 6</reference>.  <div eID="gen13722" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6b1c23be50848a11cac080ee8b9413942019d0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv28"/><title type="x-s3">Truth and Falsehood.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv28"/> <div sID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The wicked is snared by the transgression of <hi type="italic">his</hi> lips: but the just shall come out of trouble. <div eID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13724" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The wicked entangling themselves in trouble by their folly, when God in justice leaves them to themselves. They are often <hi type="italic">snared by the transgression of their lips</hi> and their throats are cut with their own tongues. By <hi type="italic">speaking evil of dignities</hi> they expose themselves to public justice; by giving ill language they become obnoxious to private resentments, are sued for defamation, and actions on the case for words are brought against them. Many a man has paid dearly in this world for the transgression of his lips, and has felt the lash on his back for want of a bridle upon his tongue, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. 2. The righteous extricating themselves out of trouble by their own wisdom, when God in mercy comes in for their succour: <hi type="italic">The just shall come out</hi> of such troubles as the wicked throw themselves headlong into. It is intimated that the just may perhaps come into trouble; but, <hi type="italic">though they fall, they shall not be utterly cast down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Ps. xxxiv. 19</reference>.
entries.3d657cb145b4af977ea848ddd2e33e5fa637e307: <div eID="gen13724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13725" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of <hi type="italic">his</hi> mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him. <div eID="gen13725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13726" type="x-p"/> We are here assured, for our quickening to every good word and work, 1. That even good words will turn to a good account (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">A man shall be satisfied with good</hi> (that is, he shall gain present comfort, that inward pleasure which is truly satisfying) <hi type="italic">by the fruit of his mouth,</hi> by the good he does with his pious discourse and prudent advice. While we are teaching others we may ourselves learn, and feed on the bread of life we break to others. 2. That good works, much more, will be abundantly rewarded: The <hi type="italic">recompence of a man's hands</hi> for all his work and labour of love, all he has done for the glory of God and the good of his generation, <hi type="italic">shall be rendered unto him,</hi> and he shall reap as he has sown. Or it may be understood of the general rule of justice; God will <hi type="italic">render to every man according to his work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.6">Rom. ii. 6</reference>.
entries.9687f986b94f26ef6e8aeb566bf9e3fe65929285: <div eID="gen13726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The way of a fool <hi type="italic">is</hi> right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise. <div eID="gen13727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13728" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What it is that keeps a fool from being wise: <hi type="italic">His way is right in his own eyes;</hi> he thinks he is in the right in every thing he does, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> asks no advice, because he does not apprehend he needs it; he is confident he knows the way, and cannot miss it, and therefore never enquires the way. The rule he goes by is to do that which is <hi type="italic">right in his own eyes,</hi> to walk in the way of his heart. <hi type="italic">Quicquid libet, licet—He makes his will his law.</hi> He is a fool that is governed by his eye, and not by his conscience. 2. What it is that keeps a wise man from being a fool; he is willing to be advised, desires to have counsel given him, and <hi type="italic">hearkens to counsel,</hi> being diffident of his own judgment and having a value for the direction of those that are wise and good. He is wise (it is a sign he is so, and he is likely to continue so) whose ear is always open to good advice.
entries.4dc226aec09054ff11c0e40052a85dd42db4fb54: <div eID="gen13728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13729" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> covereth shame. <div eID="gen13729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13730" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Passion is folly: <hi type="italic">A fool is known by his anger</hi> (so some read it); not but that a wise man may be angry when there is just cause for it, but then he has his anger under check and direction, is <hi type="italic">lord of his anger,</hi> whereas a fool's anger lords it over him. He that, when he is provoked, breaks out into indecent expressions, in words or behaviour, whose passion alters his countenance, makes him outrageous, and leads him to forget himself, <hi type="italic">Nabal</hi> certainly is his name and <hi type="italic">folly is with him. A fool's indignation is known in the day;</hi> he proclaims it openly, whatever company he is in. Or it is known in the day he is provoked; he cannot defer showing his resentments. Those that are soon angry, that are quickly put into a flame by the least spark, have not that rule which they ought to have over their own spirits. 2. Meekness is wisdom: <hi type="italic">A prudent man covers shame.</hi> (1.) He covers the passion that is in his own breast; when his <hi type="italic">spirit is stirred,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">heart hot within him,</hi> he keeps his mouth as with a bridle, and suppresses his resentments, by smothering and stifling them. Anger is shame, and, though a wise man be not perfectly free from it, yet he is ashamed of it, rebukes it, and suffers not the evil spirit to speak. (2.) He covers the provocation that is given him, the indignity that is done him, winks at it, covers it as much as may be from himself, that he may not carry his resentments of it too far. It is a kindness to ourselves, and contributes to the repose of our own minds, to extenuate and excuse the injuries and affronts that we receive, instead of aggravating them and making the worst of them, as we are apt to do.
entries.7d993b08681f2f8600b5e27e6ef410fb82c403a7: <div eID="gen13730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13731" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">He that</hi> speaketh truth sheweth forth righteousness: but a false witness deceit. <div eID="gen13731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13732" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A faithful witness commended for an honest man. <hi type="italic">He that</hi> makes conscience of <hi type="italic">speaking truth,</hi> and representing every thing fairly, to the best of his knowledge, whether in judgment or in common conversation, whether he be upon his oath or no, he <hi type="italic">shows forth righteousness;</hi> he makes it to appear that he is governed and actuated by the principles and laws of righteousness, and he promotes justice by doing honour to it and serving the administration of it. 2. A false witness condemned for a cheat; he <hi type="italic">shows forth deceit,</hi> not only how little conscience he makes of deceiving those he deals with, but how much pleasure he takes in it, and that he is possessed by a lying spirit, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.3-Jer.9.5">Jer. ix. 3-5</reference>. We are all concerned to possess ourselves with a dread and detestation of the sin of lying (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.163">Ps. cxix. 163</reference>) and with a reigning principle of honesty.
entries.7a9b847b4b63115df083f1ea49ac42352edfa1e1: <div eID="gen13732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise <hi type="italic">is</hi> health. <div eID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> The tongue is death or life, poison or medicine, as it is used. 1. There are words that are cutting and killing, that are <hi type="italic">like the piercings of a sword.</hi> Opprobrious words grieve the spirits of those to whom they are spoken, and cut them to the heart. Slanders, like a sword, wound the reputation of those of whom they are uttered, and perhaps incurably. Whisperings and evil surmises, like a sword, divide and cut asunder the bounds of love and friendship, and separate those that have been dearest to each other. 2. There are words that are curing and healing: <hi type="italic">The tongue of the wise is health,</hi> closing up those wounds which the backbiting tongue had given, making all whole again, restoring peace, and accommodating matters in variance and persuading to reconciliation. Wisdom will find out proper remedies against the mischiefs that are made by detraction and evil-speaking.
entries.ea14dd582d1e22689b6d02684b2d683bd1ac1a3c: <div eID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> but for a moment. <div eID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> Be it observed, to the honour of truth, that sacred thing, 1. That, if truth be spoken, it will hold good, and, whoever may be disobliged by it and angry at it, yet it will keep its ground. Great is the truth and will prevail. What is true will be always true; we may abide by it, and need not fear being disproved and put to shame. 2. That, if truth be denied, yet in time it will transpire. A <hi type="italic">lying tongue,</hi> that puts false colours upon things, <hi type="italic">is but for a moment.</hi> The lie will be disproved. The liar, when he comes to be examined, will be found in several stories, and not consistent with himself as he is that speaks truth; and, when he is found in a lie, he cannot gain his point, nor will he afterwards be credited. Truth may be eclipsed, but it will come to light. Those therefore that make a lie their refuge will find it a refuge of lies.  <div eID="gen13736" type="x-p"/>
entries.787d0202b7b37e333afd0ace70aa09ca09a3842d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv29"/><title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv29"/> <div sID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Deceit <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace <hi type="italic">is</hi> joy. <div eID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that devise mischief contrive, for the accomplishing of it, how to impose upon others; but it will prove, in the end, that they deceive themselves. Those that <hi type="italic">imagine evil,</hi> under colour of friendship, have their hearts full of this and the other advantage and satisfaction which they shall gain by it, but it is all a cheat. Let them imagine it ever so artfully, deceivers will be deceived. 2. Those that consult the good of their neighbours, that study the things which make for peace and give peaceable advice, promote healing attempts and contrive healing methods, and, according as their sphere is, further the public welfare, will have not only the credit, but the comfort of it. They will have joy and success, perhaps beyond their expectation. <hi type="italic">Blessed are the peace-makers.</hi>
entries.5125fd8f92a192cb52363d1e0f7575ac9a30421f: <div eID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> There shall no evil happen to the just: but the wicked shall be filled with mischief. <div eID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13740" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Piety is a sure protection. If men be sincerely righteous, the righteous God has engaged that no evil shall happen to them. He will, by the power of his grace in them, that principle of justice, keep them from the evil of sin; so that, though they be tempted, yet they shall not be overcome by the temptation, and though they may come into trouble, into many troubles, yet to them those troubles shall have no evil in them, whatever they have to others (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.10">Ps. xci. 10</reference>), for they shall be overruled to work for their good. 2. Wickedness is as sure a destruction. Those that live in contempt of God and man, that are set on mischief, with mischief they <hi type="italic">shall be filled.</hi> They shall be more mischievous, shall be <hi type="italic">filled with all unrighteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.29">Rom. i. 29</reference>. Or they shall be made miserable with the mischiefs that shall come upon them. Those that delight in mischief shall have enough of it. Some read the whole verse thus, <hi type="italic">There shall no evil happen to the just, though the wicked be filled with mischief</hi> and spite against them. They shall be safe under the protection of Heaven, though hell itself break loose upon them.
entries.8188cdecf7958749f0da05dce10f251c4a4f2377: <div eID="gen13740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Lying lips <hi type="italic">are</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but they that deal truly <hi type="italic">are</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13742" type="x-p"/> We are here taught, 1. To hate lying, and to keep at the utmost distance from it, because it is an abomination to the Lord, and renders those abominable in his sight that allow themselves in it, not only because it is a breach of his law, but because it is destructive to human society. 2. To make conscience of truth, not only in our words, but in all our actions, because those that <hi type="italic">deal truly</hi> and sincerely in all their dealings are <hi type="italic">his delight,</hi> and he is well pleased with them. We delight to converse with, and make use of, those that are honest and that we may put a confidence in; such therefore let us be, that we may recommend ourselves to the favour both of God and man.
entries.70c303a5f3e47ff0eff9193de8a7f6c77e8b374f: <div eID="gen13742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness. <div eID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He that is wise does not affect to proclaim his wisdom, and it is his honour that he does not. He communicates his knowledge when it may turn to the edification of others, but he conceals it when the showing of it would only tend to his own commendation. Knowing men, if they be prudent men, will carefully avoid every thing that savours of ostentation, and not take all occasions to show their learning and reading, but only to use it for good purposes, and then let <hi type="italic">their own works praise them. Ars est celare artem—The perfection of art is to conceal it.</hi> 2. He that is foolish cannot avoid proclaiming his folly, and it is his shame that he cannot: <hi type="italic">The heart of fools,</hi> by their foolish words and actions, <hi type="italic">proclaims foolishness;</hi> either they do not desire to hide it, so little sense have they of good and evil, honour and dishonour, or they know not how to hide it, so little discretion have they in the management of themselves, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">Eccl. x. 3</reference>.
entries.052a33e4da1f644ef47b99595b4f2a94824c7d7a: <div eID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute. <div eID="gen13745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Industry is the way to preferment. Solomon advanced Jeroboam because he saw that he was an industrious young man, and minded his business, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.28">1 Kings xi. 28</reference>. Men that take pains in study and serviceableness will thereby gain such an interest and reputation as will give them a dominion over all about them, by which means many have risen strangely. He that has been <hi type="italic">faithful in a few things</hi> shall be made <hi type="italic">ruler over many things.</hi> The elders, that <hi type="italic">labour in the word and doctrine,</hi> are <hi type="italic">worthy of double honour;</hi> and those that are diligent when they are young will get that which will enable them to rule, and so to rest, when they are old. 2. Knavery is the way to slavery: <hi type="italic">The slothful</hi> and careless, or rather the <hi type="italic">deceitful</hi> (for so the word signifies), <hi type="italic">shall be under tribute.</hi> Those that, because they will not take pains in an honest calling, live by their shifts and arts of dishonesty, are paltry and beggarly, and will be kept under. Those that are diligent and honest when they are apprentices will come to be masters; but those that are otherwise are the fools who, all their days, must be <hi type="italic">servants to the wise in heart.</hi>
entries.b8e76e188aa6bc581eb113003132c8747aaee62c: <div eID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad. <div eID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13748" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The cause and consequence of melancholy. It is <hi type="italic">heaviness in the heart;</hi> it is a load of care, and fear, and sorrow, upon the spirits, depressing them, and disabling them to exert themselves with any vigour on what is to be done or fortitude in what is to borne; it makes them stoop, prostrates and sinks them. Those that are thus oppressed can neither do the duty nor take the comfort of any relation, condition, or conversation. Those therefore that are inclined to it should watch and pray against it. 2. The cure of it: <hi type="italic">A good word</hi> from God, applied by faith, <hi type="italic">makes it glad;</hi> such a word is that (says one of the rabbin), <hi type="italic">Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee;</hi> the good word of God, particularly the gospel, is designed to make the hearts glad that are weary and heavy-laden, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Matt. xi. 28</reference>. Ministers are to be helpers of this joy.
entries.550e803830092ed4aee9b275fa7fdd053efdffd0: <div eID="gen13748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> The righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> more excellent than his neighbour: but the way of the wicked seduceth them. <div eID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. That good men do well for themselves; for they have in themselves an excellent character, and they secure to themselves an excellent portion, and in both they excel other people: <hi type="italic">The righteous is more abundant than his neighbour</hi> (so the margin); he is richer, though not in this world's goods, yet in the graces and comforts of the Spirit, which are the true riches. There is a true excellency in religion; it ennobles men, inspires them with generous principles, makes them substantial; it is an excellency which is, in the sight of God, of great price, who is the true Judge of excellency. His neighbour may make a greater figure in the world, may be more applauded, but the righteous man has the intrinsic worth. 2. That wicked men do ill for themselves; they walk in a way which <hi type="italic">seduces them.</hi> It seems to them to be not only a pleasant way, but the right way; it is so agreeable to flesh and blood that they therefore flatter themselves with an opinion that it cannot be amiss, but they will not gain the point they aim at, nor enjoy the good they hope for. It is all a cheat; and therefore the righteous is wiser and happier than his neighbour, that yet despise him and trample upon him.
entries.caaa39c6a882936801097289761d106307e06521: <div eID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The slothful <hi type="italic">man</hi> roasteth not that which he took in hunting: but the substance of a diligent man <hi type="italic">is</hi> precious. <div eID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. That which may make us hate slothfulness and deceit, for the word here, as before, signifies both: <hi type="italic">The slothful</hi> deceitful <hi type="italic">man</hi> has roast meat, but that which he roasts is not what he himself <hi type="italic">took in hunting,</hi> no, it is what others took pains for, and he lives upon the fruit of their labours, like the drones in the hive. Or, if slothful deceitful men have taken any thing by hunting (as sportsmen are seldom men of business), yet they do not roast it when they have taken it; they have no comfort in the enjoyment of it; perhaps God in his providence cuts them short of it. 2. That which may make us in love with industry and honesty, that the <hi type="italic">substance of a diligent man,</hi> though it be not great perhaps, <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet <hi type="italic">precious.</hi> It comes from the blessing of God; he has comfort in it; it does him good, and his family. It is his own daily bread, not bread out of other people's mouths, and therefore he sees God gives it to him in answer to his prayer.
entries.04c530c3c64e7a1ce93e7b1be80c7726c7e34aef: <div eID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> In the way of righteousness <hi type="italic">is</hi> life; and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the pathway <hi type="italic">thereof there is</hi> no death. <div eID="gen13753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13754" type="x-p"/> The way of religion is here recommended to us, 1. As a straight, plain, easy way; it is <hi type="italic">the way of righteousness.</hi> God's commands (the rule we are to walk by) are all holy, just, and good. Religion has right reason and equity on its side; it is a <hi type="italic">path-way,</hi> a way which God has cast up for us (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>); it is a highway, the king's highway, the King of kings' highway, a way which is tracked before us by all the saints, the good old way, full of the footsteps of the flock. 2. As a safe, pleasant, comfortable way. (1.) There is not only life at the end, but there is life in the way; all true comfort and satisfaction. The favour of God, which is better than life; the Spirit, who is life. (2.) There is not only life in it, but so as that in it <hi type="italic">there is no death,</hi> none of that sorrow of the world which works death and is an allay to our present joy and life. There is no end of that life that is in the way of righteousness. Here there is life, but there is death too. <hi type="italic">In the way of righteousness</hi> there <hi type="italic">is life, and no death,</hi> life and immortality.  <chapter eID="Prov.12"/> <div eID="gen13754" type="x-p"/>

entries.04850f6cfb7a54aff7ef4c445c7774c4c87066b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7434"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <div sID="gen11488" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.1-Prov.12.28">Pr 12:1-28</reference>.<div eID="gen11488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7434"/><hi type="bold">1. loveth knowledge--</hi>as the fruit of instruction or training (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.2">Pr 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen11489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hateth reproof--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">Pr 10:17</reference>).<div eID="gen11490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brutish--</hi>stupid, regardless of his own welfare (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Psa 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.22">73:22</reference>). <div eID="gen11491" type="x-p"/>
entries.8addc301685303fa18e8a59a75c6158894a9ea87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7435"/><div sID="gen11492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7435"/>3. entries.d685bec1cc412683205861afb74197665cbb8e18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7437"/><div sID="gen11497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7437"/><hi type="bold">5. thoughts--</hi>or, "purposes."<div eID="gen11497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are right--</hi>literally, "are judgment," that is, true decisions.<div eID="gen11498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsels--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.11.14">Pr 11:14</reference>).<div eID="gen11499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceit--</hi>contrary to truth and honesty. <div eID="gen11500" type="x-p"/>
entries.970493c4669e2d10e39dff0ccbc693cbef228623: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7438"/><div sID="gen11501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7438"/><hi type="bold">6. The words--</hi>or, "expressed designs" of the wicked are for evil purposes.<div eID="gen11501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mouth--</hi>or, "words" of the righteous delivering instead of ensnaring men. <div eID="gen11502" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b9cd29191c8bee70c42833c1e6e2e27969f19df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7439"/><div sID="gen11503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7439"/>7. Such conduct brings a proper return, by the destruction of the wicked and well-being of the righteous and his family. <div eID="gen11503" type="x-p"/>
entries.03a69d61dba49e389f649b1b7a63319c1f0cdb78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7440"/><div sID="gen11504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7440"/><hi type="bold">8. despised--</hi>as opposed to commended (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.12">Pr 11:12</reference>).<div eID="gen11504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perverse heart--</hi>or, "wicked principles," as opposed to one of wisdom. <div eID="gen11505" type="x-p"/>
entries.246fbd09891185cb87f0f9ffe3c6c0a94783978d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7441"/><div sID="gen11506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7441"/><hi type="bold">9. despised--</hi>held in little repute, obscure (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.23">1Sa 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Is 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen11506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath a servant--</hi>implying some means of honest living.<div eID="gen11507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honoureth himself--</hi>is self-conceited. <div eID="gen11508" type="x-p"/>
entries.abf24e43c0341604f6cd887caab303505480d450: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7442"/><div sID="gen11509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7442"/><hi type="bold">10. regardeth--</hi>literally, "knoweth" (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen11509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercies ... cruel--</hi>as acts of compassion ungraciously rendered to the needy. The righteous more regards a beast than the wicked a man. <div eID="gen11510" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ed6ec0979c796435e56807082cac3685a75d6df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7443"/><div sID="gen11511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7443"/>11. The idler's fate is the result of indolence and want of principle (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.32">Pr 6:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.7">7:7</reference>). <div eID="gen11511" type="x-p"/>
entries.d464b4f52dbed6fb262a4134484dbbd75746ad57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7444"/><div sID="gen11512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7444"/><hi type="bold">12. the wicked ... evil--</hi>They love the crafty arts of deception.<div eID="gen11512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the root ... fruit--</hi>their own resources supply them; or, it may be rendered: "He (God) giveth, or, sets (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22">Eze 17:22</reference>) the root of the righteous," and hence it is firm: or, the verb is impersonal; "As to the root ... it is firm" (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.19">Pr 17:19</reference>). <div eID="gen11513" type="x-p"/>
entries.53aa742f38e8a7aca430e7e5d5c818fb8588c096: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7445"/><div sID="gen11514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7445"/><hi type="bold">13-14. The wicked is snared, &c.--</hi>The sentiment expanded. While the wicked, such as liars, flatterers, &c., fall by their own words, the righteous are unhurt. Their good conduct makes friends, and God rewards them. <div eID="gen11514" type="x-p"/>
entries.3356e288cc09c45aceb72c5818835358b672cdeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7446"/><div sID="gen11515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7446"/><hi type="bold">15. The way ... eyes--</hi>The fool is self-conceited (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.12.1">Pr 12:1</reference>; 1:32; 10:17; <reference osisRef="Jas.3.17">Jas 3:17</reference>). <div eID="gen11515" type="x-p"/>
entries.a83086c4e6a7b9eb755a44d7a305d609b0b3cd84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7447"/><div sID="gen11516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7447"/><hi type="bold">16. prudent ... shame--</hi>He is slow to denounce his insulters (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.19">Jas 1:19</reference>). <div eID="gen11516" type="x-p"/>
entries.43ded47b394a093caa17e0f6003ab50276012a01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7448"/><div sID="gen11517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7448"/><hi type="bold">18. speaketh--</hi>literally, "speaketh hastily," or indiscreetly (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.33">Psa 106:33</reference>), as an angry man retorts harsh and provoking invectives.<div eID="gen11517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tongue ... health--</hi>by soothing and gentle language. <div eID="gen11518" type="x-p"/>
entries.f506d997336f275954224f12d7e3c2f24f5665f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7449"/><div sID="gen11519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7449"/>19. Words of truth are consistent, and stand all tests, while lies are soon discovered and exposed. <div eID="gen11519" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f705061b4499969f2e5963deea0473fb67089f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7450"/><div sID="gen11520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7450"/><hi type="bold">20. that imagine--</hi>or, "plan" (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.29">Pr 3:29</reference>). They design a deceitful course, to which, with all its evils and dangers to others and themselves, the happiness of peace-makers is opposed (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.5.9">Mt 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.18">Ro 12:18</reference>). <div eID="gen11520" type="x-p"/>

entries.87d17248ca1fe6d02edfe9b12f0edee36043c536: <div eID="gen24160" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24161" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24162" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24162" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24161" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24163" type="x-p"/> Of the benefit of instruction, and the cultivation of piety. The virtuous woman. The different lot of the just and unjust. The humane man. The industrious man. The fool and the wise man. The uncharitable. The excellence of the righteous. The slothful is in want. Righteousness leads to life, etc. <div eID="gen24163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24164" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24165" type="x-p"/> Whoso loveth instruction - מוסר musar, discipline or correction, loves knowledge; for correction is the way to knowledge. <div eID="gen24165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24166" type="x-p"/> But he that hateth reproof is brutish - בער baar, he is a bear; and expects no more benefit from correction than the ox does from the goad.
entries.1e0c8b19f3bebcacc272a2d94877bb615cee134d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24167" type="x-p"/> A good man obtaineth favor - First, it is God who makes him good; for every child of Adam is bad till the grace of God changes his heart. Secondly, while he walks in the path of obedience he increases in goodness, and consequently in the favor of the Lord.
entries.0ea33542c38ec930e15cf80b71138f5fb154e3b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24168" type="x-p"/> A man shall not be established by wickedness - Evil is always variable: it has no fixed principle, except the root that is in the human heart; and even that is ever assuming new forms. Nothing is permanent but goodness; and that is unchangeable, because it comes from God. The produce of goodness is permanent, because it has God's blessing in it: the fruit of wickedness, or the property procured by wickedness, is transitory, because it has God's curse in it. The righteous has his root in God; and therefore he shall not be moved.
entries.f3618f649a33cb46a0d00cf18d74cbd609cac34a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24169" type="x-p"/> A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband - אשת חיל esheth chayil, a strong woman. Our word virtue (virtus) is derived from vir, a man; and as man is the noblest of God's creatures, virtue expresses what is becoming to man; what is noble, courageous, and dignified: and as vir, a man, comes from vis, power or strength; so it implies what is strong and vigorous in principle: and as in uncivilized life strength and courage were considered the very highest, because apparently the most necessary, of all virtues; hence the term itself might have become the denomination of all excellent moral qualities; and is now applied to whatever constitutes the system of morality and moral duties. In some parts of the world, however, where arts and sciences have made little progress, strength is one of the first qualifications of a wife, where the labors of the field are appointed to them. It is not an uncommon sight in different parts of Africa, to see the wives (queens) of the kings and chiefs going out in the morning to the plantations, with their mattock in their hand, and their youngest child on their back; and when arrived at the ground, lay the young prince or princess upon the earth, which when weary of lying on one side, will roll itself on the other, and thus continue during the course of the day, without uttering a single whimper, except at the intervals in which its mother gives it suck; she being employed all the while in such labor as we in Europe generally assign to our horses. In these cases, the strong wife is the highest acquisition; and is a crown to her husband, though he be king of Bonny or Calabar. It is certain that in ancient times the women in Judea did some of the severest work in the fields, such as drawing water from the wells, and watering the flocks, etc. On this account, I think, the words may be taken literally; and especially when we add another consideration, that a woman healthy, and of good muscular powers, is the most likely to produce and properly rear up a healthy offspring; and children of this kind are a crown to their parents. <div eID="gen24169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24170" type="x-p"/> Is as rottenness in his bones - Does not this refer to a woman irregular in her manners, who by her incontinence not only maketh her husband ashamed, but contracts and communicates such diseases as bring rottenness into the bones? I think so. And I think this was the view taken of the text by Coverdale, who translates thus: "A stedfast woman is a crowne unto her hussbonde: but she that behaveth herself unhonestly is a corruption in his bones."
entries.9bbfe3a673a4ea390450cd09bf21553028628d4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24171" type="x-p"/> The wicked are overthrown - Seldom does God give such a long life or numerous offspring. <div eID="gen24171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24172" type="x-p"/> But the house of the righteous shall stand - God blesses their progeny, and their families continue long in the earth; whereas the wicked seldom have many generations in a direct line. This is God's mercy, that the entail of iniquity may be in some sort cut off, so that the same vices may not be strengthened by successive generations. For generally the bad root produces not only a bad plant, but one worse than itself.
entries.5c6176fb66c4800c55a244705d340efffcb94f7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24173" type="x-p"/> He that is despised, and hath a servant - I believe the Vulgate gives the true sense of this verse: Melior est pauper, et sufficiens sibi; quam gloriosus, et indigens pane. "Better is the poor man who provides for himself, than the proud who is destitute of bread." The versions in general agree in this sense. This needs no comment. There are some who, through pride of birth, etc., would rather starve, than put their hands to menial labor. Though they may be lords, how much to be preferred is the simple peasant, who supports himself and family by the drudgery of life!
entries.6bf3705fb692c09ac460f8c870c67e8f8ed9efb4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24174" type="x-p"/> A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast - One principal characteristic of a holy man is mercy: cruelty is unknown to him; and his benevolence extends to the meanest of the brute creation. Pity rules the heart of a pious man; he can do nothing that is cruel. He considers what is best for the comfort, ease health, and life of the beast that serves him, and he knows that God himself careth for oxen: and one of the ten commandments provides a seventh part of time to be allotted for the rest of laboring beasts as well as for man. <div eID="gen24174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24175" type="x-p"/> I once in my travels met with the Hebrew of this clause on the sign board of a public inn: יודע צדיק נפש בהמתו yodea tsaddik nephesh behemto. "A righteous man considereth the life of his beast;" which, being very appropriate, reminded me that I should feed my horse. <div eID="gen24175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24176" type="x-p"/> The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel - אחזרי achzari, are violent, without mercy, ruthless. The wicked, influenced by Satan, can show no other disposition than what is in their master. If they appear at any time merciful, it is a cloak which they use to cover purposes of cruelty. To accomplish its end, iniquity will assume any garb, speak mercifully, extol benevolence, sometimes even give to the poor! But, timeo Danaos, et dona ferentes. The cry of fire at midnight, provided it be in another's dwelling, is more congenial to their souls than the; cry of mercy. Look at the human fiends, "out-heroding Herod," in horse races, bruising matches, and cock fights, and in wars for the extension of territory, and the purposes of ambition. The hell is yet undescribed, that is suited to such monsters in cruelty.
entries.d1a5d75fa53d35c67d5c8cb7893334e9bc13121b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24177" type="x-p"/> He that tilleth his land - God's blessing will be in the labor of the honest agriculturist. <div eID="gen24177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24178" type="x-p"/> But he that followeth vain persons - He who, while he should be cultivating his ground, preparing for a future crop, or reaping his harvest, associates with fowlers, coursers of hares, hunters of foxes, or those engaged in any champaign amusements, is void of understanding; and I have known several such come to beggary. <div eID="gen24178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24179" type="x-p"/> To this verse the Septuagint add the following clause: 'ov estin en oinwn diatribaiv, en toiv eautou ocurwmasi kataleiqei atimian. "He who is a boon companion in banquets, shall leave dishonor in his own fortresses." This has been copied by the Vulgate and the Arabic. That is The man who frequents the ale-house enriches that, while he impoverishes his own habitation.
entries.f7eea50fb2d197afaf01cb9f3c49502f1e363be0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24180" type="x-p"/> The wicked desireth the net of evil men - They applaud their ways, and are careful to imitate them in their wiles.
entries.a512e4f7e719ed4eb6cc53cf027c8ef49464355b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24181" type="x-p"/> The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips - A man who deals in lies and false oaths will sooner or later be found out to his own ruin. There is another proverb as true as this: A liar had need of a good memory; for as the truth is not in him, he says and unsays, and often contradicts himself.
entries.5110a64c155da64e52f4acfffe68b5713bb2dc02: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24182" type="x-p"/> A fool's wrath is presently known - We have a proverb very like this, and it will serve for illustration: - <div eID="gen24182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24183" type="x-p"/> A fool's bolt is soon shot. <div eID="gen24183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24184" type="x-p"/> A weak-minded man has no self-government; he is easily angered, and generally speaks whatever comes first to his mind.
entries.5e414285dc75bd1804d2613c1e6a7641088e0b8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24185" type="x-p"/> There is that speaketh - Instead of בוטה boteh, blabbing out, blustering, several MSS. have בוטח boteach, Trusting: and instead of כמדקרות kemadkeroth, As the piercings, seven MSS., with the Complutensian Polyglot, have במדקרות bemadkeroth, In the piercings. "There is that trusteth in the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health." But I suppose the former to be the true reading.
entries.2420d88944434de67b3feca860e03eaef3fd4e87: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24186" type="x-p"/> A lying tongue is but for a moment - Truth stands for ever; because its foundation is indestructible: but falsehood may soon be detected; and, though it gain credit for a while, it had that credit because it was supposed to be truth.
entries.93b350d80806439bcc2fe96c294334e4be7a039b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24187" type="x-p"/> There shall no evil happen to the just - No, for all things work together for good to them that love God. Whatever occurs to a righteous man God turns to his advantage. But, on the other hand, the wicked are filled with mischief: they are hurt, grieved, and wounded, by every occurrence; and nothing turns to their profit.
entries.a4dc19d3a4ab69a2a3e8ae56c56a34796f826703: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24188" type="x-p"/> A prudent man concealeth knowledge - "If a fool hold his peace he may pass for a wise man." I have known men of some learning, so intent on immediately informing a company how well cultivated their minds were, that they have passed either for insignificant pedants or stupid asses.
entries.45069fdcf9fccd6426a9793fe864968a39f25bff: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24189" type="x-p"/> The hand of the diligent shall bear rule - And why? because by his own industry he is independent; and every such person is respected wherever found.
entries.9a3fa7dfaee2a206a821fdf123156ef6c780bf95: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24190" type="x-p"/> Heaviness in the heart of a man maketh it stoop - Sorrow of heart, hopeless love, or a sense of God's displeasure - these prostrate the man, and he becomes a child before them. <div eID="gen24190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24191" type="x-p"/> But a good word maketh it glad - A single good or favorable word will remove despondency; and that word, "Son, be of good cheer, thy sins are forgiven thee," will instantly remove despair.
entries.711ec52703736f3db44a1afdc5bd89df1b6c95cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24192" type="x-p"/> The righteous is more excellent than his neighbor - That is, if the neighbor be a wicked man. The spirit of the proverb lies here: The Poor righteous man is more excellent than his sinful neighbor, though affluent and noble. The Syriac has it, "The righteous deviseth good to his neighbor." A late commentator has translated it, "The righteous explore their pastures." How מרעהו can be translated Their pastures I know not; but none of the versions understood it in this way. The Vulgate is rather singular: Qui negligit damnum propter amicum, justus est. "He who neglects or sustains a loss for the sake of his friend, is a just man." The Septuagint is insufferable: "The well-instructed righteous man shall be his own friend." One would hope these translators meant not exclusively; he should love his neighbor as himself.
entries.d04cf8567a826562d15537698a08c854188e5515: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24193" type="x-p"/> The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting - Because he is a slothful man, he does not hunt for prey; therefore gets none, and cannot roast, that he may eat. There is some obscurity in the original on which the versions cast little light. Coverdale translates the whole verse thus: "A discreatfull man schal fynde no vauntage: but he that is content with what he hath, is more worth than golde." My old MS. Bible: The gylful man schal not fynd wynnynge: and the substance of a man schal ben the pris of gold. <div eID="gen24193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24194" type="x-p"/> By translating hymr remiyah the deceitful, instead of the slothful man, which appears to be the genuine meaning of the word, we may obtain a good sense, as the Vulgate has done: "The deceitful man shall not find gain; but the substance of a (just) man shall be the price of gold." But our common version, allowing hymr remiyah to be translated fraudulent, which is its proper meaning, gives the best sense: "The fraudulent man roasteth not that which he took in hunting," the justice of God snatching from his mouth what he had acquired unrighteously. <div eID="gen24194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24195" type="x-p"/> But the substance of a diligent man - One who by honest industry acquires all his property - is precious, because it has the blessing of God in it.
entries.16ec01e60e497749f5d77d35f10ca415759feb8c: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24196" type="x-p"/> In the way of righteousness is life - חיים chaiyim, lives; life temporal, and life eternal. <div eID="gen24196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24197" type="x-p"/> And in the pathway thereof there is no death - Not only do the general precepts and promises of God lead to life eternal, and promote life temporal; but every duty, every act of faith, patience of hope, and labor of love, though requiring much self-abasement, self-denial, and often an extension of corporal strength, all lead to life. For in every case, in every particular, "the path of duty is the way of safety." The latter clause is only a repetition of the sense of the former.  <chapter eID="Prov.12"/> <div eID="gen24197" type="x-p"/>

entries.ae7222c1c8a36d9ddfe8998d97d43f4811c7c156: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.1">Pro 12:1</reference> <div eID="gen11008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11009" type="x-p"/> Three proverbs on knowledge, the favour of God, firmness and the means thereto. 1 He loveth correction who loveth knowledge,    And he hateth instruction who is without reason. <div eID="gen11009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11010" type="x-p"/> It is difficult in such cases to say which is the relation of the ideas that is intended. The sequence of words which lies nearest in the Semitic substantival clause is that in which the predicate is placed first; but the subject may, if it is to be made prominent, stand at the head of the sentence. Here, 1b, the placing of the subject in advance recommends itself: one who hates instruction is devoid of reason. But since we have no reason in 1a to invert the order of the words as they lie together, we take the conceptions placed first in both cases as the predicates. Thus: he who loves knowledge shows and proves that he does so by this, that he willingly puts himself in the place of a learner; and devoid of reason is he who with aversion rejects reproof, which is designed to guard him from future mistakes and false steps. Regarding the punctuation דעת אהב (with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> on the ante-penult. and the העמדה-sign on the penult.), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 11:26., Pro 1:19. In 1b the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> in תוכחת is transformed from <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> (<hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, xviii. §2), as in Pro 15:10. בּער (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.30.2">Pro 30:2</reference>) is a being who is stupid as the brute cattle (בּעיר, from בּער, to graze, cattle of all kinds; Arab. b'ayr, the beast κατ ̓ ἐξ., <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the camel); as a <hi type="italic">homo brutus</hi> is compared to a בּהמּה (Ps. 49:21), 73:22), and is called Arab. behymt, from bahym, “shut up” (spec. dabb, a bear; thwr, an ox; ḥamâr, an ass) (Fl.).
entries.efb7483e938543d7149ed004542f95d1522fe2ba: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">2</reference> A good man obtaineth favour with Jahve,    But the man of wicked devices He condemns. <div eID="gen11010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11011" type="x-p"/> He who is an אישׁ מזמּות (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.17">Pro 14:17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference>) is defined in <reference osisRef="Prov.24.8">Pro 24:8</reference> : he is a man of devices, namely, that are wicked, one who contrives evil against his neighbour. The meaning of the subject-conception טוב is defined according to this, although in itself also it is clear, for טוב, used of God (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Psa 73:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">Psa 86:5</reference>) and of men (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Pro 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.14">Pro 14:14</reference>), denotes the good (<hi type="italic">bonus</hi>) in the sense of the benevolent (<hi type="italic">benignus</hi>); the Scripture truths, that God is love, that love is the essence of goodness and is the fulfilling of the law, are so conformed to reason, that they stamp themselves as immediate component parts of the human consciousness. A טוב is thus a man who acts according to the ruling motive of self-sacrificing love; such an one obtains (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on יפיק, <hi type="italic">educit</hi> = <hi type="italic">adipiscitur</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.13">Pro 3:13</reference>) the favour of God, He is and shows Himself kind to him, while on the contrary He condemns the wicked intriguer. Hitzig translates: the former of intrigues is punishable (as the Syr.: is condemned; Targ.: his contrivance is shattered to pieces); but to become a רשׁע = <hi type="italic">reus</hi> הרשׁיע does not denote, but either to practise רשׁע, <reference osisRef="Job.34.12">Job 34:12</reference>, or to set forth as רשׁע = to condemn, Isa 50:9. Taken in the former signification (Jerome, <hi type="italic">impie agit</hi>), a declaration is made which is not needed, since the moral badness already lies in the reference of the subject: thus ירשׁיע will be used also of Jahve. In proof that the poet did not need to say ואת־אישׁ, Zöckler rightly points to <reference osisRef="Prov.10.6">Pro 10:6</reference>; Job 22:29.
entries.31560efa24fc5d3af70312c9a0648d06fcbfbcec: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.3">Pro 12:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.3">3</reference> A man does not stand by wickedness,    But the root of the righteous remains unmoved. <div eID="gen11011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11012" type="x-p"/> In רשׁע there lies the idea of want of inward stay (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>); in a manner of thought and of conduct which has no stay in God and His law, there can be expected no external endurance, no solidity. The righteous, on the contrary, have their root in God; nothing can tear them from the ground in which they are rooted, they are as trees which no storm outroots. The very same thought is clothed in other words in <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">Pro 10:25</reference>, and another statement regarding the root of the righteous is found at Pro 12:12.
entries.7b0c4ebb052d49b3a353a0ffd0e33963466d2904: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.4">Pro 12:4</reference> <div eID="gen11012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11013" type="x-p"/> We now place together <reference osisRef="Prov.12.4">Pro 12:4</reference>-12. One proverb concerning the house-wife forms the beginning of this group, and four regarding the management of the house and business form the conclusion. 4 A good brave wife is the crown of her husband,    But as rottenness in his bones is one that causeth shame. <div eID="gen11013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11014" type="x-p"/> As <reference osisRef="Prov.11.16">Pro 11:16</reference> says of אושׁת חן, the pleasant wife (חן = χάρις), that she obtaineth honour, so this proverb of אושׁת חיל, the good wife (חיל = ἀρετή, <hi type="italic">virtus</hi>), that she raises her husband to higher honour: she is for his self-consciousness στέφανος καυχήσεως (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>), and is also to him such a crown of honour before the world (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.31.23">Pro 31:23</reference>). On the contrary, a מבישׁה, conducting herself shamefully (cf. regarding the double meaning of this <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> word, which only here occurs in the fem., at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.5">Pro 10:5</reference>), is to her husband <hi type="italic">instar cariei in ossibus</hi>. רקב (רקב, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.7">Pro 10:7</reference>) denotes both the <hi type="italic">caries</hi> and the worm-hole (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.41.19">Job 41:19</reference>, עץ רקּבון, worm-eaten wood). Like as the <hi type="italic">caries</hi> slowly but continuously increases, till at last the part of the body which the bone bears and the whole life of the man falls to ruin; so an unhappy marriage gnaws at the marrow of life, it destroys the happiness of life, disturbs the pursuit, undermines the life of the husband.
entries.90f8d75f5bee408d7a608c3245da22c1bd4c28fd: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.5">Pro 12:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.5">5</reference> The thoughts of the righteous are justice,    The counsels of the godless are deceit. <div eID="gen11014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11015" type="x-p"/> They are so, that is, in their contents and their aim. To the righteous are ascribed מחשׁבות, namely, simple and clear; to the godless, תּחבּות, carefully thought out, prudently thought through schemes and measures, but on that very account not simple, because with a tendency; for the righteous have an objective rule, namely, that which is right in the sight of God and of men, but the godless have only a selfish purpose, which they seek to attain by deceiving, and at the cost of, their neighbour.
entries.9bf581138cf71126c005c6e710bc117b781f5c11: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.6">Pro 12:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.6">6</reference> The word of the godless is to lie in wait for the blood of others,    But the mouth of the upright delivereth them. <div eID="gen11015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11016" type="x-p"/> Our editions have דברי רשׁעים, but the right sequence of the accents (in Cod. 1294 and elsewhere) is דברי רשׁעים; the logical relation in this transformation, which is only rhythmically conditioned, remains the same. The vocalization wavers between ארב־, which would be imper., and ארב־, which is infin., like אמר־, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.7">Pro 25:7</reference>, ענשׁ־, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.11">Pro 21:11</reference>, אכל־, Gen 3:11. However one punctuates it, the infin. is intended in any case, in which the expression always remains sketchy enough: the words of the godless are lying in wait for blood, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, they are calculated to bring others to this, into the danger of their lives, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, before the tribunal by false charges and false witness. דּם is the accus. of the object; for instead of ארב לדם (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference>), to lurk for blood, a shorter expression, ארב דּם, is used (Ewald, §282a). The suffix of יצּילם<note placement="foot">Elias Levita, in his note to the root פה in Kimchi’s Wörterbuch, reads תּצּילם, and so also do 6 codd. in Kennicot. But פּה is masculine.</note> might appear, after <reference osisRef="Prov.11.6">Pro 11:6</reference>, to refer back to the ישׁרים; but the thought that their mouth saves the upright, that they thus know to speak themselves out of the danger, is by far less appropriate (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the contrary, בדעת, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.9">Pro 11:9</reference>) than the thought that the mouth of the upright delivereth from danger those whose lives are threatened by the godless, as is rightly explained by Ewald, Bertheau, Elster. The personal subject or object is in the Mashal style often to be evolved from the connection, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.26">Pro 14:26</reference>; Pro 19:23.
entries.4f696ab24534f34906d83fcda56aace22567b00f: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.7">Pro 12:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.7">7</reference> The godless are overturned and are no more,    But the house of the righteous stands. <div eID="gen11016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11017" type="x-p"/> Bertheau and Zöckler explain: The wicked turn about, then are they no more; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as we say: it is over with them “in the turning of a hand.” The noun in the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>. may certainly be the subject, like <reference osisRef="Prov.17.12">Pro 17:12</reference>, as well as the object (Ewald, §328c), and הפך may be used of the turning about of oneself, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.9">Psa 78:9</reference>; 2Ki 5:26; 2Ch 9:12. That explanation also may claim for itself that הפך nowhere occurs with a personal object, if we except one questionable passage, Isa 1:7. But here the interpretation of the רשׁעים as the object lies near the contrast of בית, and moreover the interpretation of the הפך, not in the sense of στρέφεσθαι (lxx), but of καταστρέφειν (Syr., Targ., Jerome, <hi type="italic">Graec</hi>. <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., Luther), lies near the contrast of יעמד. The <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>. thus leaves the power from which the catastrophe proceeds indefinite, as the <hi type="italic">pass</hi>. יהפפכוּ would also leave it, and the act designedly presented in a vague manner to connect with ו the certain consequences therewith, as Pro 25:4., as if to say: there comes only from some quarter an unparalleled overthrow which overwhelms the godless; thus no rising up again is to be thought on, it is all over with them; while, on the contrary, the house of the righteous withstands the storm which sweeps away the godless.
entries.65153ec2e2d6f65653f107eed7135136342bdb3f: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">Pro 12:8</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">8</reference> According to the measure of his intelligence is a man praised,    And whoever is of a perverse mind is despised. <div eID="gen11017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11018" type="x-p"/> Everywhere in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> שׂכל has no other meaning than <hi type="italic">intellectus</hi>. The praise which is given to a man measures itself לפי שׂכלו (punctuate לפי־שׂכלו, according to <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 41, <hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, xx. §1), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, according to the measure (so לפי is used in the oldest form of the language) of his intelligence, or as we may also say, of his culture; for in these proverbs, which make the fear of God the highest principle, שׂכל means also understanding of moral excellence, not merely the intellectual superiority of natural gifts. הלּל is here a relative conception of manifold gradations, but it does not mean renown in general, but good renown. Parallel with שׂכלו, לב refers to the understanding (νοῦς); the rendering of Löwenstein, “who is of false heart,” is defective. נעוה (synon. of נפתּל and עקּשׁ, but nowhere else interchanging with it) means here a <hi type="italic">vero et recto detortus et aversus</hi> (Fl.). Such a man who has not a good understanding, nor any certain rule of judgment, falls under contempt (<hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> τῷ ὀντωτῇ εἰς μυσαγμόν, after the false reading of יהוה instead of יהיה), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he defames himself by his crooked judgment of men, of things and their relations, and is on this account in no position rightly to make use of them.
entries.cf30f1cc007ec2f41e787684a9843a488cf3bae8: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.9">Pro 12:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.9">9</reference> Better is he who is lowly and has a servant,    Than he that makes himself mighty and is without bread. <div eID="gen11018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11019" type="x-p"/> This proverb, like <reference osisRef="Prov.15.17">Pro 15:17</reference>, commends the middle rank of life with its quiet excellences. נקלה (like <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.23">1Sa 18:23</reference>), from קלה, cognate with קלל, Syr.
