'kly, to despise, properly <hi type="italic">levi pendere, levem habere</hi> (whence קלון, scorn, disgrace), here of a man who lives in a humble position and does not seek to raise himself up. Many of the ancients (lxx, Symmachus, Jerome, Syr., Rashi, Luther, Schultens) explain ועבד לו by, and is a servant to himself, serves himself; but in that case the words would have been עבד לנפשׁו (Syr. דּמשׁמּשׁ נפשׁהּ), or rather ועבדּו הוּא. ועבד לו would be more appropriate, as thus pointed by Ziegler, Ewald, and Hitzig. But if one adheres to the traditional reading, and interprets this, as it must be interpreted: <hi type="italic">et cui servus</hi> (Targ., <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet</hi>.), then that supplies a better contrast to וחסר־לחם, for “the first necessity of an oriental in only moderate circumstances is a slave, just as was the case with the Greeks and Romans” (Fl.). A man of lowly rank, who is, however, not so poor that he cannot support a slave, is better than one who boasts himself and is yet a beggar (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">2Sa 3:29</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. often expresses a striving to be, or to wish to appear to be, what the adj. corresponding to the verb states, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, התגּדּל, התעשּׁר; like the Greek middles, εζεσθαι, αζεσθαι, cf. התחכּם and σοφίζεσθαι. So here, where with Fleischer we have translated: who makes himself mighty, for כבד, <hi type="italic">gravem esse</hi>, is etymologically also the contrast of קלה. The proverb, Sirach 10:26: κρείσσων ἐργαζόμενος καὶ περισσεύων ἐν πᾶσιν, ἢ δοξαζόμενος καὶ ἀπορῶν ἄρτων (according to the text of Fritzsche), is a half remodelling, half translation of this before us.
entries.5753d51bc3dc070d32f560ec8b2523ea5eea55ab: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.10">Pro 12:10</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.10">10</reference> The righteous knows how his cattle feel,      And the compassion of the godless is cruel. <div eID="gen11019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11020" type="x-p"/> The explanation: the righteous taketh care for the life of his beast (Fl.), fails, for 10a is to be taken with <reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exo 23:9</reference>; נפשׁ signifies also the state of one’s soul, the frame of mind, the state of feeling; but ידע has, as in the related proverb, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Pro 27:23</reference>, the meaning of careful cognizance or investigation, in conformity with which one acts. If the <hi type="italic">Torâ</hi> includes in the law of the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.10">Exo 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.12">Exo 23:12</reference>) useful beasts and cattle, which are here especially meant, and secures to them the reward of their labour (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">Deu 25:4</reference>); if it forbids the mutilation, and generally the giving of unnecessary pain, to beasts; if it enjoins those who take a bird’s nest to let the dam escape (Deu 22:6.) - these are the prefigurations of that דעת נפש בהמה, and as the God of the <hi type="italic">Torâ</hi> thus appears at the close of the Book of Jonah, this wonderful apology (<hi type="italic">defensio</hi>) of the all-embracing compassion, the God also of the world-history in this sympathy for the beasts of the earth as the type of the righteous. <div eID="gen11020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11021" type="x-p"/> In 10b most interpreters find an oxymoron: the compassion of the godless is compassionless, the direct opposite of compassion; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he possesses either altogether no compassion, or he shows such as in its principle, its expression, and in its effects is the opposite of what it ought to be (Fl.). Bertheau believes that in the sing. of the predicate אכזרי he is justified in translating: the compassion of the wicked is a tyranny. And as one may speak of a loveless love, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of a love which in its principle is nothing else than selfishness, so also of a compassionless compassion, such as consists only in gesture and speech without truth of feeling and of active results. But how such a compassionless compassion toward the cattle, and one which is really cruel, is possible, it may be difficult to show. Hitzig’s conjecture, רחמי, sprang from this thought: the most merciful among sinners are cruel - the sinner is as such not רחוּם. The lxx is right in the rendering, τὰ δὲ σπλάγχνα τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνελεήμονα. The noun רחמים means here not compassion, but, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.30">Gen 43:30</reference> (lxx ἔντερα or ἔγκατα) and 1Ki 3:26 (lxx μήτρα), has the meaning the bowels (properly tender parts, cf. Arab. rakhuma, to be soft, tender, with rḥm), and thus the interior of the body, in which deep emotions, and especially strong sympathy, are wont to be reflected (cf. Hos 10:8). The singular of the predicate אכזרי arises here from the unity of the subject-conception: the inwards, as <reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jer 50:12</reference>, from the reference of the expression to each individual of the many.
entries.eb9bf941fbbbf3eebcf0d5232dacc8f29438489e: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.11">Pro 12:11</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.11">11</reference> He that tilleth his own ground is satisfied with bread,      And he that followeth after vain pursuits is devoid of understanding. <div eID="gen11021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11022" type="x-p"/> Yet more complete is the antithetic parallelism in the doublette, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.19">Pro 28:19</reference> (cf. also Sir. 20:27a). The proverb recommends the cultivation of the field as the surest means of supporting oneself honestly and abundantly, in contrast to the grasping after vain, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, unrighteous means of subsistence, windy speculations, and the like (Fl.). ריקים are here not persons (Bertheau), but things without solidity and value (lxx μάταια; Aquila, Theodotion, κενά), and, in conformity with the contrast, not real business. Elsewhere also the mas. plur. discharges the function of a neut. noun of multitude, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., נגידים, <hi type="italic">principalia</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.6">Pro 8:6</reference>, and זדים, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference> - one of the many examples of the imperfect use of the gender in Hebr.; the speaker has in ריקים, <hi type="italic">vana et inania</hi>, not אנשׁים (Jdg 9:4), but דברים (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.47">Deu 32:47</reference>) in view. The lxx erroneously at <reference osisRef="Prov.28.19">Pro 28:19</reference>, and Symmachus and Jerome at both places understand ריקים of slothfulness.
entries.5186bf505a9b269049c7c4bca27274dde21daa71: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.12">Pro 12:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.12">12</reference> The godless lusteth after the spoil of evil-doers;      But the root of the righteous shoots forth. <div eID="gen11022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11023" type="x-p"/> This translation is at the same time an explanation, and agrees with Fleischer’s “the godless strives by unrighteous gain like the wicked (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.14">Pro 4:14</reference>) to enrich himself, namely, as must be understood from the antithetic members of the parallelism, in vain, without thereby making progress and gaining anything certain. The preterite, as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.2">Pro 11:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.8">Pro 11:8</reference>, etc., places the general true proposition as a separate historic principle derived from experience. In 12b יתּן stands elliptically or pregnantly: <hi type="italic">edet</hi>, <hi type="italic">scil</hi>. <hi type="italic">quod radix edere solet, sobolem stirpis, ramorum</hi>, etc., as in the Arab. natan and ânatan are specially used without an obj. of the spontaneousness of an odour.” מצוד (from צוּד, to spy, to hunt) is elsewhere the instrument of the hunt (a net), here the object and end of it. If the words had been מצוּדי רעים, then we would explain after מלאכי רעים, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Psa 78:49</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., comm. on), and אושׁת רע, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.24">Pro 6:24</reference>; but in the difference of number, רעים will not be the qualitative but the subjective personal genitive: <hi type="italic">capturam qualem mali captant</hi>. Ewald, who understands ריקים, 11b, of good-for-nothing-fellows, interprets רעים here, on the contrary, as neuter (§172b): the desire of the wicked is an evil net, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, wherein he catches all manner of evil for himself. The lxx has here two proverbs, in which מצוד occurs in the plur. and in the sense of ὀχυρώματα; 12b of the Hebr. text is rendered: αἱ δὲ ῥίζαι τῶν εὐσεβῶν ἐν ὀχρυώμασι, which Schleusner explains <hi type="italic">immotae erunt</hi>. The Hebr. text can gain nothing from this variation. That the lxx read ושׁרשׁ צדיקים איתן is not probable, since they nowhere thus translate איתן. But Reiske and Ziegler have, like Ewald and Hitzig, combined יתּן of this proverb with יתן from איתן (Arab. wâtin), <hi type="italic">firmum, perennem esse</hi>. Hitzig translates the distich, after emending the text of 12a by the help of the lxx and the Arab.: the refuge of the wicked is crumbling clay, but the root of the righteous endures (יתן from יתן). Böttcher also reads חמר instead of חמד, and translates (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 192, l. 11): the refuge of the wicked is miry clay, but the root of the righteous holdeth fast (יתן = Arab. wâtin). But this derivation of a verb יתן is not necessary. The <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> rightly, ῥίζα δὲ δικαίων δώσει. The obj. is self-evident. Rashi reads מה שהוא ראוי ליתן והוא הפרי. So also Schultens. The root giveth, is equivalent to, it is productive in bringing forth that which lies in its nature. That the root of the righteous endures (Targ. נתקיּם) is otherwise expressed, Pro 12:3.
entries.2f25dcdb82799cda9bbff0f20244f645651ac055: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">Pro 12:13</reference> <div eID="gen11023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11024" type="x-p"/> Proverbs regarding injurious and beneficial words, wise hearing and prudent silence. 13 In the transgression of the lips there lies a dangerous snare;      The righteous escapeth from trouble. <div eID="gen11024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11025" type="x-p"/> The consecutive <hi type="italic">modus</hi> (ויּצא) is here of greater weight than <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.8">Pro 11:8</reference>, where the connection follows without it (ויּבא) from the idea of the change of place. The translation: but the righteous ... restores ויצא (ויצא), and ignores the syllogistic relation of the members of the proverb, which shows itself here (cf. the contrary, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.9">Pro 11:9</reference>) to a certain degree by ויּצא. Ewald displaces this relation, for he paraphrases: “any one may easily come into great danger by means of inconsiderate words; yet it is to be hoped that the righteous may escape, for he will guard himself against evil from the beginning.” He is right here in interpreting צרה and מוקשׁ רע as the designation of danger into which one is betrayed by the transgressions of his lips, but “inconsiderate words” are less than פּשׁע שׂפתים. One must not be misled into connecting with פּשׁע the idea of missing, or a false step, from the circumstance that פּשׁע means a step; both verbs have, it is true, the common R. פש with the fundamental idea of placing apart or separating, but פּשׁע has nothing to do with פּשׁע (step = placing apart of the legs), but denotes (as Arab. fusuwḳ fisḳ, from the primary meaning <hi type="italic">diruptio, diremtio</hi>) a sinning, breaking through and breaking off the relation to God (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.24">Pro 28:24</reference>), or even the restraints of morality (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">Pro 10:19</reference>). Such a sinning, which fastens itself to, and runs even among the righteous, would not be called פשׁע, but rather חטּאת (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.9">Pro 20:9</reference>). According to this the proverb will mean that sinful words bring into extreme danger every one who indulges in them - a danger which he can with difficulty escape; and that thus the righteous, who guards himself against sinful words, escapes from the distress (cf. with the expression, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:18</reference>) into which one is thereby betrayed. רע is the descriptive and expressive epithet to מוקשׁ (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Ecc 9:12</reference>): a bad false trap, a malicious snare, for מוקשׁ is the snare which closes together and catches the bird by the feet. This proverb is repeated at <reference osisRef="Prov.29.6">Pro 29:6</reference>, peculiarly remodelled. The lxx has after <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">Pro 12:13</reference> another distich: <div eID="gen11025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11026" type="x-p"/> He who is of mild countenance findeth mercy; <div eID="gen11026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11027" type="x-p"/> He who is litigious oppresseth souls. (נפשׁות, or rather, more in accordance with the Hebrew original: oppresseth himself, נפשׁו.)
entries.e46eff9bc2200d164a5ac466070b009e3a5ce84d: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">Pro 12:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">14</reference> From the fruit which the mouth of the man bringeth forth is he satisfied with good,      And what the hands of the man accomplish returns back to him. <div eID="gen11027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11028" type="x-p"/> The proverb finds its final verification in the last judgment (cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.12.37">Mat 12:37</reference>), but it is also illustrated in the present life. If the mouth of a man bringeth forth fruit - namely, the fruit of wholesome doctrine, of right guidance, of comforting exhortation, of peace-bringing consolation for others - this fruit is also to his own advantage, he richly enjoys the good which flows out of his own mouth, the blessing he bestows is also a blessing for himself. The same also is the case with the actions of a man. That which is done, or the service which is rendered by his hands, comes back to him as a reward or as a punishment. גּמוּל signifies primarily accomplishment, execution, and is a twofold, double-sided conception: a rendering of good or evil, and merit on the side of men (whether merited reward or merited punishment), as well as recompense, requital on the side of God. The first line is repeated, somewhat altered, at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.2">Pro 13:2</reference>; Pro 18:20. The whole proverb is prophetically echoed in Isa 3:10. The Kerı̂ ישׁיב has Jahve as the subject, or rather the subject remains undefined, and “one requites him” is equivalent to: it is requited to him. The Chethı̂b seems to us more expressive; but this use of the active with the undefined subject, instead of the passive, is certainly as much in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> style (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.21">Pro 13:21</reference>) as the development of the subject of the clause from a foregoing genitive.
entries.8917378abcff183a41b546c239cf7c10acfc92ed: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.15">Pro 12:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.15">15</reference> The way of the fool is right in his own eyes,      But the wise listeneth to counsel. <div eID="gen11028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11029" type="x-p"/> Other proverbs, like <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference>, say that generally the judgment of a man regarding his character does not go beyond a narrow subjectivity; but there are objective criteria according to which a man can prove whether the way in which he walks is right; but the fool knows not other standard than his own opinion, and however clearly and truly one may warn him that the way which he has chosen is the wrong way and leads to a false end, yet he obstinately persists;<note placement="foot">Vid., kindred proverbs by Carl Schulze, Die bibl. <hi type="italic">Sprichwörter der deutschen Sprache</hi> (1860), p. 50, and M. C. Wahl’s <hi type="italic">Das Sprichwort in der heb.-aram. Literatur, u.s.w.</hi> (1871), p. 31.</note> while a wise man is not so wise in his own eyes (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.7">Pro 3:7</reference>) as not to be willing to listen to well-meant counsel, because, however careful he may be regarding his conduct, yet he does not regard his own judgment so unerring as not to be inclined ever anew to try it and let it stand the test. Ewald has falsely construed: yet whoever hears counsel is wise. In consequence of the contrast, אויל and חכם are the subject ideas, and with ושׁמע לעצה is brought forward that which is in contrast to the self-complacency of the fool, the conduct of the wise man.
entries.52f7bba87851b3401fb53ab6f51384d1a20cafd8: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.16">Pro 12:16</reference> <div eID="gen11029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11030" type="x-p"/> The relations of the subject and the predicate are the same as in the preceding verse. <div eID="gen11030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11031" type="x-p"/> The fool makes known his vexation on the same day [at once], <div eID="gen11031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11032" type="x-p"/> On the contrary, the prudent man hideth the offence. <div eID="gen11032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11033" type="x-p"/> Very frequently in these proverbs the first line is only defined by the adducing of the second, or the second holds itself in the light of the first. A post-bibl. proverb says that a man is known by three things: by his כוס (his behaviour in drinking), his כיס (his conduct in money transactions), and his כעס (his conduct under deep inward excitement). So here: he is a fool who, if some injury is done to him, immediately shows his vexation in a passionate manner; while, on the contrary the prudent man maintains silence as to the dishonour that is done to him, and represses his displeasure, so as not to increase his vexation to his own injury. Passionless retaliation may in certain cases be a duty of self-preservation, and may appear to be necessary for the protection of truth, but passionate self-defence is always of evil, whether the injury which is inflicted be justifiable or unjustifiable. Regarding ערוּם, <hi type="italic">callidus</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 56; Schultens’ comparison of the Greek γεγυμνασμένος is only a conceit in want of better knowledge. Regarding כּסה (only here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.23">Pro 12:23</reference>) with מכסּה, as שׁחר (only <reference osisRef="Prov.11.27">Pro 11:27</reference>) with משׁחר, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ewald, §170a. בּיּום signifies on the self-same day = without delay, immediately, and is well translated by the lxx αὐθήμερον. With another object, 16b is repeated in 23a.
entries.66702b01edb2a0302898fa018f2b555af74084ae: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.17">Pro 12:17</reference> <div eID="gen11033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11034" type="x-p"/> Most of the remaining parables of this section refer to the right use and the abuse of the tongue. 17 He that breathes the love of truth, utters that which is right;      But a lying tongue, deceit <div eID="gen11034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11035" type="x-p"/> This verse is similar in meaning to <reference osisRef="Prov.14.5">Pro 14:5</reference> (where 5b = <reference osisRef="Prov.6.19">Pro 6:19</reference>); the second line of the distich = Pro 14:25. Everywhere else יפיח כּזבים stand together, only here יפיח is joined to אמוּנה; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding this יפיח forming an attributive clause, and then employed as an adjective, but with distinct verbal force, at Pro 6:19. Viewed superficially, the proverb appears tautological; it is not so, however, but places in causal connection the internal character of men and their utterances: whoever breathes אמוּנה, truth or conscientiousness (the property of the אמוּן, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, lets the voice of this be heard in his utterances, such an one speaks צדק, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, uprightness, integrity, that which is correct, right (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Isa 45:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.41.26">Isa 41:26</reference>), in relation to truth in general, and to the present case in particular; but he who עד שׁקרים, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he who, against better knowledge and the consciousness of untruth, confirms by his testimony (from עוּד, <hi type="italic">revertere</hi>, to say again and again), therewith gives utterance to his impure character, his wicked intention, proceeding from delight in doing evil or from self-interest, and diverted towards the injury of his neighbour. As אמונה and מרמה correspond as statements of the contents of the utterances, so צדק and שקרים as statements of their motive and aim. מרמה is obj. accus. of the יגּיד (from הגּיד, to bring to light, cf. נגד, visibility) to be supplied, not the pred. nom. <hi type="italic">dolorum structor</hi>, as Fleischer poetically finds.
entries.be6be7f9e782bde7b10f08293c98b16e10526573: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.18">Pro 12:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.18">18</reference> There is that babbleth like the thrusts of a sword,      But the tongue of the wise is healing. <div eID="gen11035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11036" type="x-p"/> The second (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pro 11:24</reference>) of the proverbs beginning with ישׁ. The verb בּטה (בּטא), peculiar to the Hebr., which in the modern Hebr. generally means “to speak out” (מבטא in the grammar: the pronunciation) (according to which the lxx, Syr., and Targ. translate it by אמר), means in biblical Hebr., especially with reference to the binding of oneself by an oath (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.4">Lev 5:4</reference>), and to solemn protestations (Num 30:7, Num 30:9, according to which Jerome, <hi type="italic">promittit</hi>): to utter incautiously in words, to speak without thought and at random, referred erroneously by Gesenius to the R. בט, to be hollow, probably a word imitative of the sound, like the Greek βατταρίζειν, to stammer, and βαττολογεῖν, to babble, which the lexicographers refer to a talkative person of the name of Βάττος, as our “<hi type="italic">salbadern</hi>” [= to talk foolishly] owes its origin to one Jenaer Bader on the Saal. Theod. and the <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> give the false reading בּוטח (πεποιθώς). כּמדקרות חרב stands <hi type="italic">loco accusativi</hi>, the כּ being regarded as a noun: (<hi type="italic">effutiens verba</hi>) <hi type="italic">quae sunt instar confossionum gladii</hi> (Fl.). We also call such a man, who bridles his loquacity neither by reflection nor moderates it by indulgent reference to his fellow-men, a <hi type="italic">Schwertmaul</hi> (sword-mouth) or a <hi type="italic">Schandmaul</hi> (a mouth of shame = slanderer), and say that he has a tongue like a sword. But on the other hand, the tongue of the wise, which is in itself pure gentleness and a comfort to others, since, far from wounding, rather, by means of comforting, supporting, directing exhortation, exercises a soothing an calming influence. Regarding רפא, whence מרפּא, Dietrich in Gesenius’ Lex. is right. The root-meaning of the verb רפא (cognate רפה, to be loose, <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. to let go, <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. <reference osisRef="Prov.18.9">Pro 18:9</reference>, to show oneself slothful) is, as the Arab. kindred word rafâ, rafa, raf, rawf (râf) shows, that of stilling, softening, soothing, whence arises the meaning of healing (for which the Arab. has ṭabb and 'alkh); the meaning to repair, to mend, which the Arab. rafâ and rafa have, does not stand in a prior relation to to heal, as might appear from <reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>, but is a specializing of the general idea of <hi type="italic">reficere</hi> lying in <hi type="italic">mitigare</hi>, just as the patcher is called ἀκέστρια = ἠπήτρια,<note placement="foot">Whether ῥάπτειν, explained neither by Curtius nor by Flick, stands in a relation to it, we leave out of view.</note> from ἀκέομαι, which means equally to still and to heal. Since thus in רפא the meanings of mitigating and of healing are involved, it is plain that מרפא, as it means healing (the remedy) and at the same time (cf. θεραπεία, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev 22:2</reference>) the preservation of health, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.22">Pro 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.15">Pro 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.24">Pro 16:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.1">Pro 29:1</reference>, so also may mean mildness (here and <reference osisRef="Prov.15.4">Pro 15:4</reference>), tranquillity (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.30">Pro 14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">Ecc 10:4</reference>, calm patience in contrast to violent passion), and refreshing (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.17">Pro 13:17</reference>). Oetinger and Hitzig translate here “medicine;” our translation, “healing (the means of healing),” is not essentially different from it.
entries.db1b4f928d7d57518ead38606c3087b3f3dcf023: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.19">Pro 12:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.19">19</reference> The lip of truth endures for ever,      But the lying tongue only while I wink with the eye. <div eID="gen11036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11037" type="x-p"/> None of the old translators understood the phrase ועד־ארגּיעה; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. also, which follows Kimchi’s first explanation, is incorrect: ἕως ῥήξεως, till I split (shatter) it (the tongue). Abulwalîd is nearer the correct rendering when he takes ארגיעה as a noun = רגע with <hi type="italic">He parag</hi>. Ahron b. Joseph is better in rendering the phrase by: until I make a רגע, and quite correct if רגע (from רגע = Arab. raj', which is used of the swinging of the balance) is taken in the sense of a twinkling of the eye (Schultens: <hi type="italic">vibramen</hi>); cf. Orelli’s <hi type="italic">Die hebr. Synonyme der Zeit und Ewigkeit</hi>, p. 27f., where the synonyms for a twinkling of the eye, a moment, are placed together. עד (properly progress) has in this phrase the meaning, while, so long as, and the cohortative signifies, in contradistinction to ארגיע, which may also denote an unwilling movement of the eyelids, a movement proceeding from a free determination, serving for the measurement of a short space of time, Ewald, §228a. ארגיעה, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer 49:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">Jer 50:44</reference>, where Ewald takes כי ארגיעה (when I...) in the same sense as אד־ארגיעה here, which is more appropriate than the explanation of Hitzig, who regards כי as opening the principal clause, and attaches to הרגיע the quite too pregnant signification “to need (for an action) only a moment.” The lip of truth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the lip which speaketh truth, endures for ever (for truth, אמת = אמנתּ, is just the enduring); but the tongue of falsehood is only for a moment, or a wink of the eye, for it is soon convicted, and with disgrace brings to silence; for a post-bibl. Aram. proverb says: קוּשׁטא קאי שׁקרא לא קאי, the truth endures, the lie endures not (Schabbath 104a), and a Hebrew proverb: השּׁקר אין לו רגלים, the lie has no feet (on which it can stand).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Duke’s <hi type="italic">Rabbin. Blumenlese</hi> (1844), p. 231.</note>
entries.289add25e000641a54d3578170eda245f6e3d014: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.20">Pro 12:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.20">20</reference> Deceit is in the heart of him who deviseth evil,      But those who devise peace cause joy. <div eID="gen11037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11038" type="x-p"/> Regarding the figure of forging, fabricating (lxx, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, τεκταίνειν), or of ploughing, which underlies the phrase חרשׁ רע, <hi type="italic">moliri malum</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 3:29. That deceit is in the heart of him who deviseth evil (בּלב־חרשׁי רע, as is correctly punctuated <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by Norzi) appears to be a platitude, for the חרשׁ רע is as such directed against a neighbour. But in the first place, 20a in itself says that the evil which a man hatches against another always issues in a fraudulent, malicious deception of the same; and in the second place, it says, when taken in connection with 20b, where שׂמחה is the parallel word to מרמה, that with the deception he always at the same time prepares for him sorrow. The contrast to חרשׁי רע is יועצי שׁלום si ח, and thus denotes not those who give counsel to contending parties to conclude peace, but such as devise peace, viz., in reference to the neighbour, for יעץ means not merely to impart counsel, but also mentally to devise, to resolve upon, to decree, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">2Ch 25:16</reference>; Isa 32:7.; cf. יעץ על, Jer 49:30. Hitzig and Zöckler give to שׁלום the general idea of welfare (that which is salutary), and interpret the שׂמחה as the inner joy of the good conscience. Certainly שלום (R. של, <hi type="italic">extrahere</hi>, in the sense of deliverance from trouble) means not only peace as to the external relationship of men with each other, but also both internal and external welfare. Thus it is here meant of external welfare; Hitzig rightly compares <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer 29:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Nah.1.11">Nah 1:11</reference> to the contrast between שׁלום and רע. But as מרמה is not self-deception, but the deception of another, so also שׂמחה is not the joy of those who devise the device in their hearts for the deception of others, but the joy they procure for others. Thoughts of peace for one’s neighbour are always thoughts of procuring joy for him, as thoughts of evil are thoughts of deceit, and thus of procuring sorrow for him. Thus וליועצי is an abbreviated expression for ובלב יועצי.
entries.5728654642f65ae78676fb0207a3cda2b157aafe: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.21">Pro 12:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.21">21</reference> No evil befalls the righteous,      But the godless are full of evil. <div eID="gen11038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11039" type="x-p"/> Hitzig translates און “sorrow,” and Zöckler “injury;” but the word signifies evil as ethical wickedness, and although it may be used of any misfortune in general (as in בּן־אוני, opp. בּנימין); thus it denotes especially such sorrow as is the harvest and product of sin, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pro 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.4">Isa 59:4</reference>, or such as brings after it punishment, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.7">Hab 3:7</reference>; Jer 4:15. That it is also here thus meant the contrast makes evident. The godless are full of evil, for the moral evil which is their life-element brings out of itself all kinds of evil; on the contrary, no kind of evil, such as sin brings forth and produces, falls upon the righteous. God, as giving form to human fortune (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.13">Exo 21:13</reference>), remains in the background (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.91.10">Psa 91:10</reference> with Psa 5:1.); <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding אנה, the weaker power of ענה, to go against, to meet, to march against, Fleischer, Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterbuch</hi>, 572.
entries.3a3ace140fa4ba4582afcb8316e917fea0195614: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.22">Pro 12:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.22">22</reference> Lying lips are an abhorrence to Jahve,      And they that deal truly are His delight. <div eID="gen11039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11040" type="x-p"/> The frame of the distich is like <reference osisRef="Prov.11.1">Pro 11:1</reference>, Pro 11:20. אמוּנה is probity as the harmony between the words and the inward thoughts. The lxx, which translates ὁ δὲ ποιῶν πίστεις, had in view עשה אמונים (עשׂה אמוּנים, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.26.2">Isa 26:2</reference>); the text of all other translations agrees with that commonly received.
entries.70c4961f5ef2da48fb14d9128fbfba7ce4f025fa: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.23">Pro 12:23</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.23">23</reference> A prudent man conceals knowledge,      And a heart-fool proclaims imbecility. <div eID="gen11040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11041" type="x-p"/> In 23a <reference osisRef="Prov.12.16">Pro 12:16</reference> is repeated, only a little changed; also 16a corresponds with 23a, for, as is there said, the fool knows not how to keep his anger to himself, as here, that a heart-fool (cf. the lying mouth, 22a) proclaims (trumpets forth), or as <reference osisRef="Prov.13.16">Pro 13:16</reference> says, displays folly without referring to himself the <hi type="italic">si tacuisses</hi>. To this forward charlatan blustering, which intends to preach wisdom and yet proclaims in the world mere folly, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, nonsense and imbecility, and thereby makes itself troublesome, and only to be laughed at and despised, stands in contrast the relation of the אדם ערוּם, <hi type="italic">homo callidus</hi>, who possesses knowledge, but keeps it to himself without bringing it forth till an occasion presents itself for setting it forth at the right place, at the right time, and to the right man. The right motive also regulates such silence as well as modesty. But this proverb places it under the point of view of prudence.
entries.66e62000af43a736b4161b2bbd0b8e043a38a532: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.24">Pro 12:24</reference> <div eID="gen11041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11042" type="x-p"/> We take <reference osisRef="Prov.12.24-Prov.12.28">Pro 12:24-28</reference> together as a group. In these verses the subject is the means of rising (in the world), and the two ways, the one of which leads to error, and the other to life. 24 The land of the diligent attains to dominion,      But slothfulness will become tributary. <div eID="gen11042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11043" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference> רמיּה was adj., but to כּף standing beside it; here it is to be regarded as adj. to יד (sluggish hand) supplied from 24a, but may be equally regarded as a subst. (slothfulness) (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Pro 12:27</reference>). Regarding חרוּץ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 211. מס signifies tribute and service, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, tributary service rendered to a master. In <reference osisRef="Prov.11.29">Pro 11:29</reference> עבד stands for it. It is still the experience of to-day, as it was of Solomon’s time, that slothfulness (indolence) brings down to a state of servitude, if not even deeper, but that vigorous activity raises to dominion or to the position of a master, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to independence, wealth, respect, and power.
entries.435f207b5349d4b1fbafb2bcac5afe261b1c636e: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.25">Pro 12:25</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.25">25</reference> Trouble in the heart of a man boweth it down,      And a friendly word maketh it glad. <div eID="gen11043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11044" type="x-p"/> The twofold anomaly that דּאגה is construed as masc. and לב as fem. renders the text doubtful, but the lxx, Syr., Targum, which introduce another subject, φοβερὸς λόγος (דּבר מדאיג?), do not improve it; Theodotion’s is preferable, who translates μέριμνα ἐν καρδίᾳ ἀνδρὸς κατίσχει αὐτόν, and thus reads ישׁחנּוּ. But the rhyme is thereby lost. As כּבוד, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.6">Gen 49:6</reference>, so also may לב be used as fem., for one thereby thinks on נפשׁ; the plur. לבּות (לבבות), according to which in <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.30">Eze 16:30</reference> we find the sing. לבּה, may also conform to this. And ישׁחנה as pred. to דאגה follows the scheme <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference>, perhaps not without attractional co-operation after the scheme קשׁת גברים חתים, 1Sa 2:4. השׁחה, from שׁחה, occurs only here; but השׁח, from שׁחח, occurs only twice. דּבר טוב designates in the book of Joshua and in Kings (1Ki 8:56) the divine promise; here it is of the same meaning as 1Ki 12:7 : an appeasing word. Who has not in himself had this experience, how such a word of friendly encouragement from a sympathizing heart cheers the sorrowful soul, and, if only for a time, changes its sorrow into the joy of confidence and of hope!
entries.400c824ecc2aeac480baeff378369234a8d4abf7: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.26">Pro 12:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.26">26</reference> The righteous looketh after his pastures,      But the way of the godless leadeth them into error. <div eID="gen11044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11045" type="x-p"/> In 26a no acceptable meaning is to be gained from the traditional mode of vocalization. Most of the ancients translate יתר as part. to יתר, as it occurs in post-bibl. Hebr., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, חבּה יתרה, prevailing, altogether peculiar love. Thus the Targum, טב מן הבריהּ; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. πεπερίττευται (after Kimchi); on the other hand, Aquila, active: περισσεύων τὸν πλησίον (making the neighbour rich), which the meaning of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> as well as the form יתר oppose; Luther, “The righteous man is better than his neighbour,” according to which Fleischer also explains, “Probably יתר from יתר, πλεονάζειν, has the meaning of πλέον ἔχων, πλεονεκτῶν, he gains more honour, respect, riches, etc., than the other, viz., the unrighteous.” Yet more satisfactory Ahron b. Joseph: not the nobility and the name, but this, that he is righteous, raises a man above others. In this sense we would approve of the <hi type="italic">praestantior altero justus</hi>, if only the two parts of the proverb were not by such a rendering wholly isolated from one another. Thus יתר is to be treated as the fut. of התיר. The Syr. understands it of right counsel; and in like manner Schultens explains it, with Cocceius, of intelligent, skilful guidance, and the moderns (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Gesenius) for the most part of guidance generally. Ewald rather seeks (because the proverb-style avoids the placing of a fut. verb at the commencement of the proverb but cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.10">Pro 17:10</reference>) to interpret יתר as a noun in the sense of director, but his justification of the fixed ā is unfounded. And generally this sense of the word is exposed to many objections. The verb תּוּר signifies, after its root, to go about, “to make to go about,” but is, however, not equivalent to, to lead (wherefore Böttcher too ingeniously derives יתר = יאתר from אתר = אשׁר); and wherefore this strange word, since the Book of Proverbs is so rich in synonyms of leading and guiding! The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. התיר signifies to send to spy, Jdg 1:23, and in this sense the poet ought to have said יתר לרעהוּ: the righteous spies out (the way) for his neighbour, he serves him, as the Targum-Talmud would say, as תּיּר. Thus connected with the obj. accus. the explanation would certainly be: the righteous searches out his neighbour (Löwenstein), he has intercourse with men, according to the maxim, “<hi type="italic">Trau schau wem</hi>.” But why not רעהוּ, but מרעהוּ, which occurs only once, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.7">Pro 19:7</reference>, in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi>, and then for an evident reason? Therefore, with Döderlein, Dathe, J. D. Michaelis, Ziegler, and Hitzig, we prefer to read מרעהוּ; it is at least not necessary, with Hitzig, to change יתר into יתר, since the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> may have the force of the intens. of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, but יתר without the jussive signification is a poetic licence for יתיר. That תור can quite well be used of the exploring of the pasture, the deriv. יתוּר, <reference osisRef="Job.39.18">Job 39:18</reference>, shows. Thus altered, 26a falls into an appropriately contrasted relation to 26b. The way of the godless leads them into error; the course of life to which they have given themselves up has such a power over them that they cannot set themselves free from it, and it leads the enslaved into destruction: the righteous, on the contrary, is free with respect to the way which he takes and the place where he stays; his view (regard) is directed to his true advancement, and he looketh after his pasture, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, examines and discovers, where for him right pasture, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the advancement of his outer and inner life, is to be found. With מרעהוּ there is a combination of the thought of this verse with the following, whose catch-word is צידו, his prey.
entries.efae386f12d68d8836e12dc28f4c2d4d97bd01a6: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Pro 12:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">27</reference> The slothful pursues not his prey;      But a precious possession of a man is diligence. <div eID="gen11045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11046" type="x-p"/> The lxx, Syr., Targ., and Jerome render יחרך in the sense of obtaining or catching, but the verbal stem חרך nowhere has this meaning. When Fleischer remarks, חרך, ἅπ. λεγ., probably like לכד, properly to entangle in a noose, a net, he supports his opinion by reference to חרכּים, which signifies lattice-windows, properly, woven or knitted like a net. But חרך, whence this חרכים, appears to be equivalent to the Arab. kharḳ, <hi type="italic">fissura</hi>, so that the plur. gives the idea of a manifoldly divided (lattice-like, trellis-formed) window. The Jewish lexicographers (Menahem, Abulwalîd, Parchon, also Juda b. Koreish) all aim at that which is in accord with the meaning of the Aram. חרך, to singe, to roast (= Arab. ḥark): the slothful roasteth not his prey, whether (as Fürst presents it) because he is too lazy to hunt for it (Berth.), or because when he has it he prepares it not for enjoyment (Ewald). But to roast is צלה, not דרך, which is used only of singeing, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the hair, and roasting, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, ears of corn, but not of the roasting of flesh, for which reason Joseph Kimchi (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.) understands צידו of wild fowls, and יחרך of the singeing of the tips of the wings, so that they cannot fly away, according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates οὐ μενεῖ ... ἡ θήρα αὐτοῦ. Thus the Arab. must often help to a right interpretation of the ἅπ. λεγ.. Schultens is right: <hi type="italic">Verbum</hi> ḥarak, חרך, <hi type="italic">apud Arabes est movere, ciere, excitare</hi>, κινεῖν <hi type="italic">generatim, et speciatim excitare praedam e cubili</hi>, κινεῖν τήν θήραν. The Lat. <hi type="italic">agitare</hi>, used of the frightening up and driving forth of wild beasts, corresponds with the idea here, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, used by Ovid, Metam. x. 538, of Diana:<hi type="italic">Aut pronos lepores aue celsum in cornua cervum Aut agitat damas.</hi> <div eID="gen11046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11047" type="x-p"/> Thus יחרך together with צידו gains the meaning of hunting, and generally of catching the prey. רמיּה is here incarnate slothfulness, and thus without ellipse equivalent to אישׁ רמיה. That in the contrasted clause חרוץ does not mean ἀποτόμως, decreed (Löwenstein), nor gold (Targ., Jerome, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.), nor that which is excellent (Syr.), is manifest from this contrast as well as from <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>; Pro 12:24. The clause has from its sequence of words something striking about it. The lxx placed the words in a difference order: κτῆμα δὲ τίμιον ἀνὴρ καθαρὸς (חלוץ in the sense of Arab. khâlaṣ). But besides this transposition, two others have been tried: הון אדם חרוץ יקר, the possession of an industrious man is precious, and הון יקר אדם חרוץ, a precious possession is that (supply הון) of an industrious man. But the traditional arrangement of the words gives a better meaning than these modifications. It is not, however, to be explained, with Ewald and Bertheau: a precious treasure of a man is one who is industrious, for why should the industrious man be thought of as a worker for another and not for himself? Another explanation advanced by Kimchi: a valuable possession to men is industry, has the twofold advantage that it is according to the existing sequence of the words, and presents a more intelligible thought. But can חרוּץ have the meaning of חריצוּת (the being industrious)? Hitzig reads חרוץ, to make haste (to be industrious). This is unnecessary, for we have here a case similar to <reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">Pro 10:17</reference>, where שׁמר for שׁומר is to be expected: a precious possession of a man is it that, or when, he is industrious, חרוּץ briefly for היותו חרוּץ rof yl. The accentuation fluctuates between והון־אדם יקר (so <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Cod. 1294), according to which the Targum translates, and והון־אדם יקר, which, according to our explanation, is to be preferred.
entries.a5e01dc936187e1329d768809d70c6f296706e44: <reference osisRef="Prov.12.28">Pro 12:28</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.28">28</reference> In the path of righteousness is life,      And the way of its path is immortality. <div eID="gen11047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11048" type="x-p"/> All the old versions to the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. give אל־ instead of אל־, and are therefore under the necessity of extracting from ודּרך נתיבה a meaning corresponding to this, εἰς θάνατον, in which they are followed by Hitzig: “a devious way leadeth to death.” But נתיב (נתיבה) signifies step, and generally way and street (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.15">Pro 1:15</reference>), not “devious way,” which is expressed, Jdg 5:6, by ארחות עקלקלות. And that אל is anywhere punctuated thus in the sense of אל is previously improbable, because the Babylonian system of punctuation distinguishes the negative אל with a short <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, and the prepositional אל (Arab. ilâ) with a short <hi type="italic">Chirek</hi>, from each other (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pinsker, Einl. p. xxii.f.); the punctuation <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.16">2Sa 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.3">Jer 51:3</reference>, gives no support to the opinion that here אל is vocalized thus in the sense of אל, and it is not to be thus corrected. Nothing is more natural than that the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> in its constant contrast between life and death makes a beginning of expressing the idea of the ἀθανασία, which Aquila erroneously read from the אל־מות, Ps. 48:15. It has been objected that for the formation of such negative substantives and noun-adjectives לא (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, לא־אל, לא־עם) and not אל is used; but that אל also may be in close connection with a noun, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.13">2Sa 1:13</reference> shows. There אל־טל is equivalent to אל יהי טל, according to which it may also be explained in the passage before us, with Luther and all the older interpreters, who accepted אל in its negative signification: and on (the בּ governing) the way ... is no death. The negative אל frequently stands as an intensifying of the objective לא; but why should the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, which has already shown itself bold in the coining of new words, not apply itself to the formation of the idea of immortality?: the idol name אליל is the result of a much greater linguistic boldness. It is certain that אל is here not equivalent to אל; the Masora is therefore right in affirming that נתיבה is written with <hi type="italic">He raphatum pro mappicato</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 31a, and in the <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.), cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.20">1Sa 20:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Böttcher, §418. Thus: the way of their step is immortality, or much rather, since דּרך is not a fixed idea, but also denotes the going to a distance (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the journey), the behaviour, the proceeding, the walk, etc.: the walking (the stepping over and passing through) of their way is immortality. Rich in synonyms of the way, the Hebrew style delights in connecting them with picturesque expressions; but דּרך always means the way in general, which divides into ארחות or נתיבות (<reference osisRef="Job.6.18">Job 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.5">Jer 18:5</reference>), and consists of such (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa 3:16</reference>). The distich is synonymous: on the path of righteousness (accentuate בארח צדקה) is life meeting him who walks in it, and giving itself to him as a possession, and the walking in its path is immortality (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.17">Pro 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.28">Pro 10:28</reference>); so that to go in it and to be immortal, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to be delivered from death, to be exalted above it, is one and the same thing. If we compare with this, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sa 14:32</reference>, it is obvious that the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> begins (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 410) to break through the limits of this present life, and to announce a life beyond the reach of death.  <chapter eID="Prov.12"/> <div eID="gen11048" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="19">19. The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>d</ns0:hi> The speaker of truth is constant, and always agreeable to himself, and his words the more and longer they are tried, the more doth the truth of them appear, whereas Liars, though they may make a fair shew for a season, yet are easily and quickly convicted of falshood.</ns0:note>
